entities.name: Sames II Theosebes Dikaios
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sames II Theosebes Dikaios was the second king of Commagene. He ruled from approximately 116 to 108 BCE and was known for his diplomatic efforts with Rome.

Born into a royal family, Sames succeeded his father Ptolemaeus of Commagene as the ruler of Commagene in 116 BCE. He implemented various reforms, including the establishment of a new capital city, Samosata, which became a center of culture and learning under his rule.

Sames' diplomatic efforts with Rome led to the signing of several treaties, including the Treaty of Nisaea in 113 BCE, which granted Commagene autonomy. However, this also led to increased Roman influence in the region and eventually, the annexation of Commagene by Rome in 63 BCE.

Despite his efforts to maintain Commagene's independence, Sames' reign was marked by power struggles with his own family members and the rising influence of Rome. His legacy as a skilled diplomat and statesman continues to be studied by historians today.

The discovery of the 'Samosata Inscription', which mentions Sames II Theosebes Dikaios as one of its authors, has provided valuable insights into his reign and the culture of Commagene during that time. This inscription is now housed at the British Museum, a testament to the enduring legacy of this enigmatic king.

Sames II Theosebes Dikaios' story serves as a fascinating example of the complexities of ancient geopolitics and the delicate balance between independence and influence. His reign highlights the intricate web of alliances and rivalries that defined the ancient world.
